content: Scurvy, also known as scorbutus, is a deficiency disease caused by an inadequate intake of vitamin C, which is essential for proper collagen synthesis in humans. The term ascorbic acid, the scientific name for vitamin C, is derived from the Latin name for scurvy, scorbutus. The clinical manifestations of scurvy include the development of liver spots on the skin, spongy gums, and bleeding from mucous membranes. These spots are most commonly observed on the thighs and legs. Affected individuals often appear pale, experience depression, and may suffer from partial immobility. In advanced stages, scurvy can lead to the formation of open, suppurating wounds and the loss of teeth. Historically, scurvy was prevalent among sailors, pirates, and soldiers who were deprived of fresh fruits and vegetables for extended periods. Hippocrates described the disease as early as 460–380 BC, and its cause and treatment have been recognized in various native cultures since prehistoric times. For instance, in 1536, French explorer Jacques Cartier utilized the knowledge of local natives to save his crew from scurvy by boiling the needles of the arbor vitae tree (Eastern White Cedar) to make a tea rich in vitamin C. The Scottish surgeon James Lind, in 1753, was the first to scientifically demonstrate that scurvy could be treated with citrus fruits. His findings were published in his book A Treatise of the Scurvy. In infants, scurvy is sometimes referred to as Barlow's disease, named after Sir Thomas Barlow, a British physician who described the condition. Other eponyms for scurvy include Moeller's disease and Cheadle's disease. Scurvy is caused by a lack of vitamin C, which is destroyed during pasteurization. Infants fed on ordinary bottled milk without adequate vitamin supplementation are at risk. Commercially available baby formulas now include added vitamin C to prevent this. Human breast milk contains sufficient vitamin C, provided the mother has an adequate intake. Scurvy is one of the diseases associated with malnutrition and remains widespread in regions reliant on external food aid. Although rare, cases of scurvy have been documented in individuals with poor dietary choices in industrialized nations. From a historical perspective, scurvy was likely first identified as a disease by Hippocrates. During the 13th century, Crusaders frequently suffered from scurvy, and it caused significant losses during wartime sieges. Scurvy was a major limiting factor in marine travel, often resulting in high mortality rates among passengers and crew on long voyages. It even played a role in World War I. By 1614, the British medical profession recognized that the acidic principle of citrus fruits was essential to prevent scurvy, though they mistakenly believed any acid could suffice. John Woodall, Surgeon General of the East India Company, recommended fresh food or citrus fruits like oranges, lemons, and limes as a cure in his 1614 book The Surgion's Mate. In 1734, Johann Bachstrom, a physician based in Leiden, published a book asserting that scurvy was caused by the absence of fresh vegetables and greens and advocated for their use as a cure. However, it was not until 1747 that James Lind formally proved that scurvy could be treated and prevented by supplementing the diet with citrus fruits. Despite James Cook's successful circumnavigation of the globe without losing a single man to scurvy, his methods, including a diet of sauerkraut and malt wort, did not consistently prevent the disease. British sailors continued to suffer from scurvy during the American Revolutionary period, particularly in the Channel Fleet. The eradication of scurvy from the Royal Navy was achieved during the Napoleonic Wars, thanks to Gilbert Blane, chairman of the Navy's Sick and Hurt Board, who implemented the use of fresh lemons as prescribed by Bachstrom and Lind. Other navies soon adopted this successful approach. The term scurvy grass originated from its observed efficacy in treating scurvy, though it was of limited use during long sea voyages. Sauerkraut was also found to be largely ineffective in preventing scurvy. During the Royal Navy's Arctic expeditions in the 19th century, it was erroneously believed that scurvy could be prevented by good hygiene, regular exercise, and crew morale, rather than a diet rich in fresh food. Consequently, scurvy continued to afflict these expeditions, even though fresh meat was known to be an effective antiscorbutic among civilian whalers and Arctic explorers. By the time of Robert Falcon Scott's Antarctic expeditions in the early 20th century, the prevailing medical theory attributed scurvy to tainted canned food. It was not until 1932 that the connection between vitamin C and scurvy was definitively established. The Royal Navy's use of limes to prevent scurvy led to the term limey as a nickname for British sailors, which later extended to all British individuals in American slang. From a pathophysiological perspective, normal collagen synthesis requires the hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues in the endoplasmic reticulum to form hydroxyproline and hydroxylysine. The enzymes prolyl and lysyl hydroxylase, which catalyze this hydroxylation, depend on ascorbic acid (vitamin C) for proper function. Without ascorbic acid, these enzymes cannot hydroxylate proline and lysine, resulting in defective collagen synthesis. Scurvy can be differentiated from other diseases by its risk factors, including advanced age, alcoholism, mental illness, infants on processed milk without supplementation, unusual dietary habits, osteoporosis, osteomalacia, osteogenesis imperfecta, multiple myeloma, homocystinuria, and hypermetabolic resorptive osteoporosis. Untreated scurvy is invariably fatal. However, since recovery only requires the resumption of normal vitamin C intake, death from scurvy is rare in modern times. The disease can be prevented by consuming a diet rich in vitamin C, found in citrus fruits like oranges and lemons, as well as other fruits such as blackcurrants, guava, kiwi, papaya, tomatoes, and strawberries. Vegetables like bell peppers, broccoli, potatoes, cabbage, spinach, and paprika are also good sources. Nutritional supplements and even some candies containing vitamin C are widely available to prevent scurvy.
